title: Esther, Daniel and Going Home
bigQuestion: How do the last books of the Ketuvim tell about speaking up, staying strong far from home, and going home again?

story.title: Noise Every Time the Villain Is Named
story.kicker: A whole room stamps, rattles and boos each time one name is read from a scroll.
paragraphs: It is a winter night in a synagogue on the North Side of Chicago. Sofia is dressed as a queen with a paper crown. Her little brother is a lion. Grown-ups are wearing silly hats. Everyone holds a noisemaker. Sofia's is a wooden rattle called a grogger.

A reader unrolls a scroll. It is not the Torah. It is the scroll of Esther, the Megillah. The reader begins to chant. The story is about a king in Persia, a brave queen and a man who wanted to hurt the Jews. That man's name is Haman.

The first time the reader says "Haman," the room explodes. People stamp their feet. Groggers rattle. Kids shout "Boo!" Sofia spins her rattle as fast as she can. Then the reader waits. When it is quiet, the story goes on. It happens again. And again. Haman's name is read more than fifty times.

Sofia's grandmother leans over. "We make noise so the villain's name is drowned out," she says. "And we laugh, because the story ends with the Jews safe." Sofia thinks about that. The scroll is very old. The noise is new every year.

After the reading, there are cookies shaped like triangles and bags of treats for neighbors. There is also a box for gifts to people who are poor. Sofia's teacher told her both are part of the holiday. The holiday is called Purim. And it all comes from one short book.
story.think: Why do you think people make noise at Haman's name instead of just listening quietly to the story?

lessons.title: A Queen in Persia
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Esther tells how a Jewish queen in Persia and her cousin Mordecai saved their people from Haman's plan.
reading: The book of *Esther* is a story set in Persia. The king is named Ahasuerus. He rules from a city called Shushan. When his queen, Vashti, refuses to come to his party, he sends her away. He looks for a new queen. He chooses a young Jewish woman named Esther. Her Hebrew name is Hadassah.

Esther's cousin *Mordecai* raised her. He tells her not to say she is Jewish. The king's top helper is *Haman*. Haman wants everyone to bow to him. Mordecai will not bow. Haman gets angry. He makes a plan to kill all the Jews in the kingdom. He picks the day by casting lots. The word for lots is *pur*.

Mordecai tells Esther about the plan. Esther is afraid. Going to the king without being called can mean death. But she fasts for three days and goes. The king welcomes her. At a dinner, she tells him about Haman's plan. The king is furious. Haman is punished, and the Jews are allowed to defend themselves. The book is only ten chapters long.

words.d: the Jewish queen of Persia in the Ketuvim who saved her people; her Hebrew name is Hadassah
Esther's cousin, who raised her and would not bow to Haman
the king's helper who planned to kill the Jews in the book of Esther
a lot, like a rolled die; Haman cast lots to pick a day, and the holiday Purim is named for it

look.title: Who Is Who in Shushan
look.text: Ahasuerus is the king. Vashti is the queen who says no. Esther is the new queen. Mordecai is Esther's cousin who will not bow. Haman is the helper who wants everyone to bow. Put these five people in the order they matter to the story's big problem.
look.prompt: Which one person's choice starts the trouble? Which one person's choice ends it? Explain.

check.q: Where is the story of Esther set?
check.why: Esther is set in Persia, in the city of Shushan, under King Ahasuerus.

check.q: Why does Haman get angry at Mordecai?
choices: Mordecai will not bow to him
check.why: Haman wants everyone to bow. Mordecai refuses, and Haman plans to kill all the Jews.

check.q: What does the word "pur" mean?
choices: A lot, like a rolled die
check.why: Pur means a lot. Haman cast lots to choose the day, and the holiday Purim takes its name from this.

lessons.title: For Such a Time as This
lessons.mainIdea: Mordecai's words to Esther ask whether she became queen so she could speak up, and readers have long noticed that God's name is never written in the book.
reading: The turning point of Esther is a message. Mordecai sends word to Esther in the palace. He says she cannot stay silent. If she does, help will come from somewhere else, but she and her family will be lost. Then he asks a question. Who knows if she became queen for such a time as this?

Esther answers with a plan. She asks all the Jews in Shushan to *fast* with her for three days. To fast means to go without food. Then she says she will go to the king, even if it is against the law. Her words are, "if I perish, I perish." That means she is ready to die if she must.

Readers notice something strange about this book. God's name is never written in it. Not once. Jewish tradition reads God as hidden in the story, working behind the scenes. The name Esther even sounds like a Hebrew word for "hidden." Other readers see a story about brave people making choices. The book lets both readings stand.

words.d: to go without food for a time, often to pray or think hard
kept out of sight; some readers say God is hidden in the book of Esther

look.title: Mordecai's Question
look.text: And who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?
look.cite: Esther 4:14, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "Come to royal estate" means "become queen." What is Mordecai asking Esther to think about? Have you ever been in the right place at the right time to help?

check.q: What does Esther ask the Jews of Shushan to do before she goes to the king?
check.why: Esther asks everyone to fast with her for three days. Then she goes to the king uninvited.

check.q: What is unusual about the book of Esther?
choices: It is the longest book in the Bible
God's name is never written in it
check.why: God's name does not appear in Esther. Jewish tradition reads God as hidden in the story.

check.q: What does "if I perish, I perish" mean?
choices: Esther is ready to die if she must
Esther is asking for a new dress
check.why: To perish means to die. Esther means she will go to the king even if it costs her life.

lessons.title: Purim: Reading the Megillah
lessons.mainIdea: On Purim, Jews read the Megillah, make noise at Haman's name, share treats, give to the poor and dress up.
reading: The book of Esther ends by setting up a holiday. It is called *Purim*, after the lots Haman cast. It comes in late winter, in the Hebrew month of Adar. Chapter 9 says the day should be one of feasting and gladness, of sending food to friends and gifts to the poor.

On Purim, Jews read the whole book of Esther out loud from a scroll. The scroll is called the *Megillah*. Each time the reader says Haman's name, people make noise with rattles called groggers. Many people wear costumes. Children and grown-ups both dress up.

Families send bags of treats to friends and neighbors. This is called mishloach manot. They also give money or food to people in need. Many eat triangle cookies with a sweet filling. Esther is one of five short books called the Five Megillot. Each one is read on its own holiday.

words.d: the holiday in late winter that remembers the story of Esther; named for the lots Haman cast
a scroll; the scroll of Esther read on Purim
five short books in the Ketuvim that are each read on a holiday

look.title: The Five Scrolls
look.cite: The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917; holidays as Jewish tradition keeps them
look.prompt: Which scroll is the shortest? Which is the longest? How many chapters are in all five together?

check.q: In which Hebrew month does Purim come?
check.why: Purim comes in Adar, in late winter. Passover is in Nisan; Tisha B'Av is in Av.

check.q: What is the Megillah read on Purim?
check.why: On Purim the scroll of Esther, the Megillah, is read out loud from beginning to end.

check.q: Which of these does Esther chapter 9 say to do on Purim?
choices: Send food to friends and gifts to the poor
check.why: Esther 9:22 says the day is for feasting, sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor.

lessons.title: Four Friends Far From Home
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Daniel tells of young Jews in Babylon who keep their ways while serving a foreign king.
reading: The book of *Daniel* begins in Babylon. The king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, has taken young people from Jerusalem to his palace. Daniel and his three friends are among them. Their friends' Hebrew names are Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. The palace gives them new Babylonian names.

The palace wants them to eat the king's rich food. Daniel asks for vegetables and water instead. He wants to keep the food rules he learned at home. He asks for a ten-day test. After ten days, the story says, the four look healthier than the others. Daniel also becomes known for explaining dreams.

Later, the king builds a huge gold statue. He orders everyone to bow to it. Daniel's three friends refuse. They are thrown into a hot furnace. The story says they walk out unharmed. Part of the book of Daniel is written in *Aramaic*, a language close to Hebrew that many people spoke in Babylon.

words.d: the book in the Ketuvim about young Jews in Babylon who stay true to their ways
the great city and kingdom that took many people from Jerusalem far from home
a language close to Hebrew; part of Daniel is written in it

look.title: The Ten-Day Test
look.text: Daniel 1 says Daniel asked the palace helper for a test: give us vegetables and water for ten days, then look at us next to the young men who eat the king's food. The helper agreed. Daniel was in a new country, with a new name, far from his family.
look.prompt: What did Daniel want to keep from home? Why might he ask for a test instead of just refusing the food?

check.q: Where does the book of Daniel take place?
check.why: Daniel and his friends are taken from Jerusalem to Babylon. Shushan is the setting of Esther.

check.q: What does Daniel ask to eat instead of the king's food?
check.why: Daniel asks for vegetables and water for a ten-day test, to keep the food rules from home.

check.q: What language is part of the book of Daniel written in?
check.why: Part of Daniel is in Aramaic, a language close to Hebrew that many spoke in Babylon.

lessons.title: The Lions' Den
lessons.mainIdea: Daniel keeps praying even when a new law forbids it, and the story says he is kept safe in the lions' den.
reading: Years pass, and a new king rules. The book calls him Darius. Daniel is one of his top helpers. Other helpers are jealous. They know Daniel prays three times a day. So they trick the king into signing a *law*. For thirty days, no one may pray to anyone but the king.

Daniel hears about the law. He goes home and prays anyway, by an open window facing Jerusalem. The jealous men catch him. The king is sad, but the law cannot be changed. Daniel is thrown into a *den* full of lions. A stone is put over the top.

The king cannot sleep. At sunrise he runs to the den and calls out. Daniel answers. The story says an angel shut the lions' mouths. Daniel is lifted out without a scratch. Jewish tradition places Daniel in the Ketuvim, with the Writings. Christian Bibles place it with the prophets. Same book, different shelf.

words.d: a rule made by a ruler or a government that everyone must follow
a pit or cave where wild animals live

look.title: Daniel Answers From the Den
look.text: Daniel calls up to the king from the den. He says his God sent an angel who shut the lions' mouths, so they did not hurt him, because he had done no wrong before God or before the king.
look.cite: Daniel 6:23 (6:22 in some Bibles), The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Daniel says he did no wrong to the king even though he broke the king's law. How can both things be true?

check.q: Why do the other helpers trick the king into making a new law?
choices: They want to move to Jerusalem
check.why: The helpers are jealous of Daniel. They know he prays every day, so they make praying against the law.

check.q: What does Daniel do after the law is signed?
choices: He stops praying for thirty days
He asks the king to change the law
He keeps praying by his window as before
check.why: Daniel keeps praying three times a day by his open window, facing Jerusalem.

check.q: Where is the book of Daniel placed in the Tanakh?
choices: It is not in the Tanakh
check.why: In the Tanakh, Daniel is in the Ketuvim. Christian Bibles place it with the prophets instead.

sections.title: A Sad Poem and a Wise Poem

lessons.title: Lamentations and Tisha B'Av
lessons.mainIdea: Lamentations is a sad poem about Jerusalem after Babylon burned the Temple, and Jews read it on Tisha B'Av.
reading: In 586 BCE, the army of Babylon burned the Temple in Jerusalem. The city was left empty. The book of *Lamentations* is five poems about that terrible time. Its Hebrew name is *Eikhah*, which means "How!" The first verse asks how the busy city became so lonely, like a widow.

The poems are carefully made. Four of the five chapters go through the Hebrew alphabet. Each verse starts with the next letter, from the first to the last. It is like grief from A to Z. Jewish tradition says the prophet Jeremiah wrote the book. Scholars say the writer lived through the disaster.

Jews read Lamentations on *Tisha B'Av*, the ninth day of the month of Av. It is a sad day in summer. People fast. They sit on the floor or on low stools. The lights are kept low, and the book is chanted in a sad tune. Tradition says the Second Temple was also destroyed on this day, by Rome in 70 CE.

words.d: five sad poems about Jerusalem after the Temple was burned; in Hebrew, Eikhah
the Hebrew name of Lamentations; it means "How!"
the ninth day of the month of Av, a fast day that remembers the burning of the Temple

look.title: How the City Sits Alone
look.text: How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! How is she become as a widow!
look.cite: Lamentations 1:1, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "Solitary" means alone. The poem pictures the city as a person. What feeling does the picture of a widow give the reader?

check.q: What happened in 586 BCE?
choices: Babylon burned the Temple in Jerusalem
Cyrus let the people go home
check.why: In 586 BCE the army of Babylon burned the Temple. Lamentations mourns that time.

check.q: What does the Hebrew name Eikhah mean?
check.why: Eikhah means "How!" It is the first word of Lamentations.

check.q: On which day is Lamentations read?
check.why: Lamentations is read on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, a fast day that remembers the Temple's destruction.

lessons.title: Ecclesiastes and Sukkot
lessons.mainIdea: Ecclesiastes says that life is short like a breath and that there is a time for everything, and Jews read it on Sukkot.
reading: The book of *Ecclesiastes* is a wise, thoughtful poem. Its Hebrew name is *Kohelet*, the name of the speaker. The first verse connects him with a son of David who was king in Jerusalem. Jewish tradition says this is Solomon. The speaker has tried everything: riches, work, fun, learning. He says it all passes like a breath.

The most famous part is chapter 3. It says there is a season for everything and a time for every purpose. A time to be born and a time to die. A time to weep and a time to laugh. A time to mourn and a time to dance. The lines come in pairs, one after another.

Jews read Ecclesiastes on *Sukkot*, the fall harvest holiday. On Sukkot, families eat in a small hut with a roof of branches. The hut is a reminder that things do not last. Kohelet says the same thing. But he also says to enjoy your bread and your work. The book ends by saying to respect God and keep the commandments.

words.d: a thoughtful book in the Ketuvim that says life passes like a breath; in Hebrew, Kohelet
the Hebrew name of Ecclesiastes and of its speaker
the fall harvest holiday when families eat in a hut with a roof of branches

look.title: A Time for Everything
look.text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
look.cite: Ecclesiastes 3:1, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Chapter 3 goes on: a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. Write two pairs of your own, like "a time to run and a time to rest."

check.q: What is the Hebrew name of Ecclesiastes?
check.why: Kohelet is the Hebrew name of Ecclesiastes and of its speaker. Eikhah is Lamentations; Mishlei is Proverbs.

check.q: On which holiday is Ecclesiastes read?
check.why: Ecclesiastes is read on Sukkot, the fall harvest holiday with huts of branches.

check.q: What does Kohelet say about riches, work and fun?
choices: They make a person a king
They all pass like a breath
check.why: Kohelet has tried everything and says it all passes like a breath. Still, he says to enjoy your bread and your work.

lessons.title: Cyrus Opens the Door
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Ezra says King Cyrus of Persia let the exiles go home to Jerusalem to rebuild the Temple.
reading: For about fifty years, many Jews lived far from home in Babylon. This time is called the *exile*. Then Persia beat Babylon. The new king was Cyrus. The book of *Ezra* opens with a message from Cyrus. He says the LORD has told him to build a house in Jerusalem. Anyone who wants to may go up and help.

Scholars date this message to about 538 BCE. Thousands of people went back. They carried the gold and silver cups that Babylon had taken from the old Temple. They laid the new foundation. Old people who remembered the first Temple cried. Young people shouted for joy. The book says the two sounds mixed together.

The work was slow. Neighbors did not want the Temple built. Work stopped for years. Two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, told the people to keep going. The *Second Temple* was finished around 515 BCE. Ezra and Nehemiah are counted as one book in the Tanakh. Together they tell the story of going home.

words.d: being forced to live far from your home country
a scribe and teacher of the Torah; also the book that tells of the return from Babylon
the Temple rebuilt in Jerusalem after the exile, finished around 515 BCE

look.title: Going Home, in Years
rows: Cyrus says the exiles may go home
look.cite: Dates as most scholars give them; Ezra 1, Ezra 6, Nehemiah 6, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the burning of the First Temple and Cyrus's message? Remember, BCE years count down.

check.q: Which king said the exiles could go home to Jerusalem?
check.why: The book of Ezra opens with Cyrus of Persia saying the exiles may go up to Jerusalem and build.

check.q: What is exile?
choices: Being forced to live far from home
check.why: Exile means being forced to live far from your home country. Many Jews were in exile in Babylon.

check.q: About when was the Second Temple finished?
check.why: Scholars date the finishing of the Second Temple to about 515 BCE. Rome destroyed it in 70 CE.

lessons.title: Nehemiah's Wall and a Big Reading
lessons.mainIdea: Nehemiah led the people to rebuild Jerusalem's wall, and Ezra read the Torah aloud so that everyone could understand it.
reading: *Nehemiah* worked for the king of Persia. He heard that Jerusalem's wall was broken and its gates were burned. He was so sad that the king noticed. Nehemiah asked to go and fix it. The king said yes. Nehemiah rode to Jerusalem and looked at the wall at night.

Then he got everyone to work. Families each built the part of the wall near their own house. Some people tried to stop them. So workers held a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other. The book says the wall was finished in fifty-two days.

When the wall was done, the people gathered in a square. Ezra the *scribe* stood on a wooden platform. He read from the Torah from morning until noon. Helpers explained the words so everyone understood. People cried, but the leaders said it was a day to rejoice and share food. Then they built huts and kept Sukkot.

words.d: the leader who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall; also the book that tells his story
a person who copies and teaches written texts; Ezra was a scribe of the Torah

look.title: Reading So Everyone Understands
look.text: And they read in the book, in the Law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
look.cite: Nehemiah 8:8, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: "Gave the sense" means explained the meaning. Why was explaining as important as reading? How is this like a teacher reading aloud today?

check.q: How long does the book say it took to rebuild the wall?
check.why: Nehemiah 6:15 says the wall was finished in fifty-two days.

check.q: What did Ezra do in the square?
choices: He read the Torah aloud while helpers explained it
check.why: Nehemiah 8 says Ezra read the Torah from a wooden platform, and helpers gave the sense so people understood.

check.q: What is a scribe?
choices: A person who copies and teaches written texts
check.why: A scribe copies and teaches written texts. Ezra was a scribe who taught the Torah.

lessons.title: The Last Book: Let Him Go Up
lessons.mainIdea: Chronicles retells the whole story and ends the Tanakh with Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem.
reading: The Tanakh ends with the book of *Chronicles*. In Hebrew it is *Divrei HaYamim*, "the words of the days." It is a retelling. It starts with Adam and lists many names. Then it tells the story of David, Solomon and the kings of Judah again. It gives extra attention to the Temple and its music.

Chronicles ends where Ezra begins. Its last verses give Cyrus's message. The very last words are "let him go up." So the Tanakh ends with an open door and a journey home. A Christian Old Testament puts the books in a different order and ends with the prophet Malachi.

Think of the whole Ketuvim. It holds songs, sayings, hard questions, love poems, a brave queen, a man among lions, a sad poem, a wise poem and the story of going home. Jewish tradition reads every one of these books at its own time of year. Together they close the Hebrew Bible with hope.

words.d: the last book of the Tanakh; it retells the story from Adam to Cyrus
the Hebrew name of Chronicles; it means "the words of the days"

look.title: The Last Words of the Tanakh
look.text: In the final verse, Cyrus says that the LORD has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem. Whoever belongs to the LORD's people, may God be with him, and let him go up.
look.cite: 2 Chronicles 36:23, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: Why might it matter that the last word of the whole Tanakh is about going up to Jerusalem, not about a disaster?

check.q: Which book comes last in the Tanakh?
check.why: The Tanakh ends with Chronicles. A Christian Old Testament ends with Malachi instead.

check.q: What are the last words of Chronicles?
check.why: 2 Chronicles 36:23 ends with Cyrus's words, "let him go up," a call to return to Jerusalem.

check.q: Where does Chronicles begin its retelling?
check.why: Chronicles starts with Adam and long lists of names before telling of David and the kings.

review.q: Which two people would not bow, one to Haman and one to a gold statue?
review.why: Mordecai refused to bow to Haman in Esther. Daniel's three friends refused to bow to the statue in Daniel 3.

review.q: What is the Megillah read on Purim?
review.why: On Purim the scroll of Esther, the Megillah, is read aloud, with noise at Haman's name.

review.q: Lamentations is read on which day?
review.why: Lamentations mourns the burning of the Temple and is read on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av.

review.q: Where does the book of Daniel take place?
review.why: Daniel and his friends are taken to Babylon. Shushan is where Esther lived.

review.q: Who let the exiles go home to Jerusalem, according to Ezra 1?
review.why: The book of Ezra opens with the message of Cyrus, king of Persia, letting the exiles go up.

review.q: "To every thing there is a season" comes from which book?
review.why: Ecclesiastes 3:1 says there is a season for everything. The book is read on Sukkot.

review.q: What did Ezra do when the wall was finished?
choices: He cast lots for a holiday
He read the Torah aloud so all could understand
review.why: Nehemiah 8 tells how Ezra read the Torah from a platform while helpers explained it.

review.q: The Tanakh ends with which words?
choices: How doth the city sit solitary
review.why: Chronicles, the last book, ends with Cyrus's words, "let him go up."
